stem: The inorganic matter of a living cell is grouped into prime elements, secondary elements and trace elements. Which set of elements forms the prime elements?

stem: A monosaccharide obeys the general formula (CH2O)n and one of its molecules contains 10 hydrogen atoms. To which series does this sugar belong, and how many oxygen atoms does one molecule contain?

distractor_rationale.A: The series is worked out correctly but the oxygen count is taken equal to the hydrogen count instead of half of it.

options.A: Z is maltose, and its hydrogen to oxygen ratio is 2:1
options.B: Z is sucrose, and its hydrogen to oxygen ratio is greater than 2:1
options.C: Z is lactose, and its hydrogen to oxygen ratio is 1:1
options.D: Z is sucrose, and its hydrogen to oxygen ratio is 2:1

correct_answer_text: Z is sucrose, and its hydrogen to oxygen ratio is 2:1

stem: The normal level of glucose in human blood is about 90 mg per 100 ml of blood. Taking this level, what mass of glucose is present in a total blood volume of 5 litres?

distractor_rationale.A: This is the amount in one litre of blood; the total volume of 5 litres has not been used.

options.C: X has 9 hydrogen atoms and Y has more than 9

options.A: Cannabinol is a phenolic synthesised from simple sugars, and glucosinolates give wine and chocolate their astringency
options.B: Cannabinol is a terpene synthesised from simple sugars, and glucosinolates are used as food preservatives
options.C: Cannabinol is a nitrogen-containing metabolite synthesised from mevalonic acid, and glucosinolates give chocolate its astringency
options.D: Cannabinol is a terpene synthesised from mevalonic acid, and glucosinolates give cabbage its flavour and protect it from pests

correct_answer_text: Cannabinol is a terpene synthesised from mevalonic acid, and glucosinolates give cabbage its flavour and protect it from pests

distractor_rationale.A: Cannabinol is a terpene and not a phenolic, and astringency in wine and chocolate is due to tannins rather than to glucosinolates.
distractor_rationale.B: The group of cannabinol is right but its precursor is mevalonic acid, and it is the antibiotics that serve as food preservatives.
distractor_rationale.C: The precursor is right but cannabinol belongs to the terpenes, and astringency in chocolate is due to tannins.

solution: Cannabinol belongs to the terpenes, which are synthesised from mevalonic acid, while glucosinolates are the compounds that give cabbage its characteristic flavour and guard it against pests.
formula_principle: Cannabinol is a terpene formed from mevalonic acid; glucosinolates are the secondary metabolites responsible for the flavour of cabbage and for its protection from pests.
common_misconception: Students assign cannabinol to the nitrogen-containing group because of its use as a drug, and credit glucosinolates with the astringency that belongs to tannins.

concept_tested: Quantitative expression of the catalytic property using the sucrase figure
stem: Sucrase can hydrolyse about 100000 times its own weight of sucrose. A purified preparation contains 1 mg of sucrase. The mass of sucrose that this preparation can hydrolyse is about:

distractor_rationale.A: Obtained by using a factor of 10000 instead of 100000, or by dropping one power of ten while converting milligram to gram.
distractor_rationale.C: Obtained by multiplying by 1000 rather than 100000, a common slip when the milligram to gram conversion factor is used as the catalytic factor.
distractor_rationale.D: Obtained by carrying one extra power of ten, treating the factor as one million times the enzyme weight.

solution: 1 mg multiplied by 100000 gives 100000 mg of sucrose. Since 1000 mg make 1 g, this is 100 g of sucrose, which shows how a very small quantity of enzyme acts on a very large quantity of substrate.
formula_principle: Catalytic property of enzymes expressed quantitatively: mass of substrate acted upon equals the catalytic factor multiplied by the mass of enzyme, with 1 g equal to 1000 mg.

concept_tested: Recognising reversibility of action and specificity of action from described enzyme behaviour
stem: An enzyme catalyses the conversion of compound X into compound Y and also catalyses the conversion of Y back into X, and it acts on no substrate other than X and Y. Which two properties of enzymes are illustrated together by this behaviour?

options.A: Catalytic property and sensitivity to pH
options.B: Reversibility of action and specificity of action
options.C: Specificity of action and sensitivity to temperature
options.D: Reversibility of action and proteinaceous nature

correct_answer_text: Reversibility of action and specificity of action

distractor_rationale.A: Nothing in the description varies the pH of the medium, and the catalytic property alone does not account for the enzyme refusing all other substrates.
distractor_rationale.C: Specificity is correctly picked up, but no temperature is altered in the description, so sensitivity to temperature is not demonstrated.
distractor_rationale.D: Reversibility is correctly picked up, but the proteinaceous nature of the enzyme is a fact of composition and is not shown by the reactions described.

concept_tested: Dependence of catalytic ability on the three-dimensional conformation bearing the active site
stem: Rule: the catalytic ability of an enzyme depends on its three-dimensional conformation, which carries the active site. A globular enzyme is treated so that its three-dimensional folding is completely lost, while every peptide bond in the chain remains intact. What is the expected consequence?

options.A: The enzyme loses its catalytic ability, because the active site no longer exists
options.B: The enzyme retains its catalytic ability, because no peptide bond in the chain has been broken
options.C: The enzyme retains its catalytic ability but loses its specificity of action
options.D: The enzyme is converted into a cofactor for another enzyme

correct_answer_text: The enzyme loses its catalytic ability, because the active site no longer exists

distractor_rationale.B: Treats catalytic ability as a property of the unbroken chain itself; the chapter ties activity to the three-dimensional conformation that carries the active site, not merely to intact peptide bonds.
distractor_rationale.C: Assumes catalysis and specificity reside in different parts of the molecule, whereas both depend on the same active site formed by the folded conformation.
distractor_rationale.D: Cofactors are inorganic ions loosely attached to the protein part of a conjugated enzyme, so an unfolded protein cannot become one.

solution: The active site is created by the specific three-dimensional folding of the enzyme. Once that folding is lost the active site no longer exists, so the enzyme cannot bind its substrate or catalyse the reaction, even though the chain of amino acid residues is unbroken.
formula_principle: Structure and function relationship in enzymes: the active site is a feature of the folded three-dimensional conformation, so loss of that conformation abolishes catalytic ability even with the chain intact.
common_misconception: Students equate an intact polypeptide chain with an intact enzyme and expect activity to survive as long as no bond in the chain is broken.
difficulty_basis: Multi-part interpretation, pathway reasoning or calculation linking several facts with plausible traps

concept_tested: Distinguishing a prosthetic group from a coenzyme by the nature of its attachment
stem: Rule: a conjugated enzyme carries a non-protein component in addition to its protein part, and the different kinds of non-protein component are told apart by the manner of their attachment. In one such enzyme the non-protein component is joined to the protein component by chemical bonds and cannot be separated from it without breaking those bonds. This component is best described as:

distractor_rationale.B: Coenzymes are described as tightly attached, and the word tightly tempts the student here, but attachment by chemical bonds that must be broken to separate the component is the description reserved for the prosthetic group.
distractor_rationale.C: Cofactors are inorganic ions loosely attached to the protein part, which is the opposite of firm attachment through chemical bonds.
distractor_rationale.D: An activator is an inorganic substance that raises enzyme activity when supplied to the reaction, not a bound component of the enzyme molecule.

concept_tested: The essential difference of the induced fit model from the lock and key model
stem: Which statement expresses the essential difference of the induced fit model of Koshland from the earlier lock and key model?

options.A: The substrate alters its own shape so as to fit an unchanging active site
options.B: The approach of the substrate brings about a change in the conformation of the enzyme
options.C: The active site is already exactly complementary to the substrate before the substrate arrives
options.D: The enzyme acts on the substrate without forming an enzyme-substrate complex

correct_answer_text: The approach of the substrate brings about a change in the conformation of the enzyme

concept_tested: Detecting the induced fit idea wrongly imported into the lock and key model
stem: Rule: in the lock and key model only a key of the correct size and shape fits into the key hole. A student states that this model explains enzyme action by the enzyme changing its shape to accommodate the substrate. The correct evaluation of that statement is that it is:

options.A: Correct, because the key hole of the lock must widen a little before the key can enter it
options.B: Incorrect, because the lock and key model denies that any enzyme-substrate complex is formed at all
options.C: Incorrect, because a change of shape in the enzyme on substrate approach belongs to Koshland's model
options.D: Correct, because the two models describe the same conformational change in different words

stem: Enzymes P and Q act on the same substrate. Under identical conditions the Km of P is 2 x 10^-5 moles per litre and the Km of Q is 4 x 10^-3 moles per litre. Which conclusion follows?

options.A: Q has the greater affinity, because its Km value is the numerically larger of the two
options.B: P and Q must have equal affinity, because Km is fixed by the substrate and both act on the same one
options.C: Q attains half of its maximum velocity at a lower substrate concentration than P does
options.D: P has the greater affinity, because a lower substrate concentration gives half maximal velocity

correct_answer_text: P has the greater affinity, because a lower substrate concentration gives half maximal velocity

distractor_rationale.A: Reads a high Km as high affinity; the chapter states that a low Km means high affinity and a high Km means low affinity.
distractor_rationale.B: Treats Km as a property of the substrate; two enzymes acting on the same substrate can and do have different Km values.
distractor_rationale.C: Misreads the powers of ten: 4 x 10^-3 is the higher concentration, so Q needs more substrate, not less, to reach half maximal velocity.

solution: The Km of P, 2 x 10^-5 moles per litre, is lower than the Km of Q, 4 x 10^-3 moles per litre. P therefore reaches half of its maximum velocity at a much smaller supply of substrate, which is what high affinity for the substrate means.
formula_principle: Low Km means high affinity of the enzyme for its substrate and high Km means low affinity, because Km is the substrate concentration needed for half of the maximum velocity.
common_misconception: Students associate a larger number with a stronger property and so read the larger Km as the greater affinity, and they also compare 2 and 4 without comparing the powers of ten.
difficulty_basis: Multi-part interpretation, pathway reasoning or calculation linking several facts with plausible traps

concept_tested: State of the enzyme when substrate concentration equals Km
stem: An enzyme has a Km of 5 x 10^-4 moles per litre for its substrate, a value lying within the range of 10^-5 to 10^-2 moles reported for most enzymes. In an assay the substrate concentration is held at exactly 5 x 10^-4 moles per litre. At this concentration the enzyme is:

options.A: 50 per cent saturated with substrate and working at its maximum velocity
options.B: 50 per cent saturated with substrate and working at half of its maximum velocity
options.C: Completely saturated with substrate and working at half of its maximum velocity
options.D: 25 per cent saturated with substrate and working at half of its maximum velocity

correct_answer_text: 50 per cent saturated with substrate and working at half of its maximum velocity

distractor_rationale.A: Maximum velocity is reached only when the enzyme is saturated; at half saturation the velocity is half of the maximum.
distractor_rationale.C: Complete saturation would require a substrate concentration well above Km, and it corresponds to the maximum velocity, not to half of it.
distractor_rationale.D: Halves the saturation a second time; the chapter links Km directly with 50 per cent saturation of the enzyme with substrate.

solution: Km is by definition the substrate concentration producing half of the maximum velocity, and it corresponds to 50 per cent saturation of the enzyme with substrate. Since the assay concentration equals Km, both conditions hold together.
formula_principle: At a substrate concentration equal to Km the enzyme is 50 per cent saturated with substrate and the reaction runs at half of its maximum velocity.
common_misconception: Students separate the velocity statement from the saturation statement and pair half maximal velocity with full saturation, or full velocity with half saturation.
difficulty_basis: One comparison, short interpretation or routine calculation linking up to two prescribed facts

concept_tested: Interpreting the plateau of the substrate concentration curve as enzyme saturation
stem: The figure shows initial enzyme velocity plotted against substrate concentration while enzyme quantity, temperature and pH are constant. What accounts for the final, almost horizontal part of the curve?

options.A: The enzyme has begun to lose its conformation because the substrate concentration is very high
options.B: The substrate has been completely used up, so no further product can be formed in the assay
options.C: The reverse reaction has begun to run at a rate equal to that of the forward reaction
options.D: All the active sites of the fixed quantity of enzyme present are occupied by substrate

correct_answer_text: All the active sites of the fixed quantity of enzyme present are occupied by substrate

distractor_rationale.A: Loss of conformation follows unsuitable temperature or pH, both of which are held constant here; an excess of substrate does not unfold the enzyme.
distractor_rationale.B: The initial velocity is measured in each case, and the flat part of the curve lies at the highest substrate concentrations, where substrate is most plentiful.
distractor_rationale.C: A reverse reaction would show as a loss of product rather than as a ceiling on the initial velocity; the flat part reflects saturation of the enzyme.

solution: As substrate concentration rises, more and more active sites are occupied, so velocity climbs steeply at first. Once the fixed quantity of enzyme is saturated, no free active site is left, and further substrate leaves the velocity unchanged, which is why the curve becomes almost parallel to the x axis.
formula_principle: Effect of substrate concentration on enzyme activity: with the enzyme quantity fixed, velocity against substrate concentration is a rectangular hyperbola whose final phase is a plateau set by saturation of the enzyme.
common_misconception: Students read the plateau as exhaustion of the substrate or as damage to the enzyme, rather than as saturation of a limited number of active sites.

concept_tested: Interpreting the rise and the sharp fall of the temperature curve of enzyme activity
stem: The figure shows the activity of a mammalian enzyme plotted against temperature while pH and substrate concentration are controlled. Which explanation of the curve is correct?

options.A: The optimum is 37 degree C, and above 40 degree C the enzyme denatures rapidly, most enzymes being destroyed at 60 to 70 degree C
options.B: The optimum is 65 degree C, and the fall in activity before it is caused by exhaustion of the substrate in the assay mixture
options.C: The rise reflects an increasing Km, and the fall begins once the Km of the enzyme has been exceeded by the temperature
options.D: The steep fall above 37 degree C occurs because heating shifts the pH of the medium away from the optimum for the enzyme

correct_answer_text: The optimum is 37 degree C, and above 40 degree C the enzyme denatures rapidly, most enzymes being destroyed at 60 to 70 degree C

distractor_rationale.B: Substrate is in large excess, and 65 degree C lies within the 60 to 70 degree C band in which most enzymes are destroyed, so it cannot be an optimum.
distractor_rationale.C: Km is a substrate concentration characteristic of the enzyme, not a temperature threshold, so it cannot mark the point at which activity falls.
distractor_rationale.D: The pH is held at the optimum throughout the experiment, so the loss of activity must be traced to the enzyme protein itself.

solution: Activity rises with temperature up to the optimum, which for reactions at normal mammalian body temperature is 37 degree C, the optimum range for most enzymes being 20 to 35 degree C. Beyond about 40 degree C the enzyme denatures rapidly, and by 60 to 70 degree C most enzymes are destroyed, which is why activity is negligible at 65 degree C.
formula_principle: Effect of temperature on enzyme activity: 37 degree C is the optimum for enzymatic reactions at normal mammalian body temperature, enzymes denature rapidly above 40 degree C, and most enzymes are destroyed at 60 to 70 degree C.
common_misconception: Students take the highest temperature at which any activity is seen, or the last point on the curve, as the optimum, and they look for causes outside the enzyme for the fall in activity.
difficulty_basis: Multi-part interpretation, pathway reasoning or calculation linking several facts with plausible traps

concept_tested: Identifying enzymes from their optimum pH values
stem: Two enzymes listed in the prescribed account are assayed over a range of pH values, with the temperature, the enzyme concentration and the substrate concentration identical in the two sets. One enzyme shows its maximum activity at pH 2 and the other at pH 9.5. The two enzymes are respectively:

distractor_rationale.B: Interchanges the two optima; the chapter gives pH 2 for pepsin and pH 9.5 for trypsin.
distractor_rationale.C: The first assignment is right, but the optimum of pH 9.5 is given for trypsin, and no pH optimum is given for amylase.
distractor_rationale.D: Both assignments fail: trypsin has its optimum at pH 9.5, not at pH 2, and no pH optimum is given for sucrase.

solution: Pepsin has its optimum at pH 2 and trypsin at pH 9.5, so the enzyme peaking in strongly acidic conditions is pepsin and the one peaking in alkaline conditions is trypsin.
formula_principle: Effect of pH on enzyme activity: each enzyme works best at a particular pH, pepsin having an optimum at pH 2 and trypsin at pH 9.5.
common_misconception: Students remember that the two enzymes have very different pH optima but cannot recall which enzyme takes the acidic value, and so reverse the pair.
difficulty_basis: One comparison, short interpretation or routine calculation linking up to two prescribed facts

concept_tested: Predicting which alterations of the reaction conditions lower enzyme activity
stem: An enzyme-catalysed reaction runs steadily at 37 degree C at the optimum pH, with substrate present in large excess. Four further assays are set up, each differing from this control in one respect only. In I a further quantity of the same enzyme is added. In II an inorganic activator is added. In III the temperature is raised to 65 degree C. In IV an inhibitor is added. In how many of the four assays is the activity expected to be LOWER than in the control?

distractor_rationale.A: Counts the inhibitor alone and overlooks that 65 degree C lies within the 60 to 70 degree C band in which most enzymes are destroyed.
distractor_rationale.C: Counts the addition of extra enzyme or of an activator as depressing activity, whereas an activator is an inorganic substance that increases enzyme activity.
distractor_rationale.D: Assumes that every departure from the control conditions must lower activity, ignoring that an activator raises it.

solution: Raising the temperature to 65 degree C places the enzyme in the 60 to 70 degree C band in which most enzymes are destroyed, so activity falls, and an inhibitor by definition reduces enzyme activity, so activity falls there too. Adding more of the same enzyme does not depress activity, and an inorganic activator increases it. Hence two assays show lower activity than the control.
formula_principle: Factors affecting enzyme activity: enzyme concentration, temperature with destruction of most enzymes at 60 to 70 degree C, and other substances, namely activators which increase activity and inhibitors which reduce it.
common_misconception: Students treat any change made to a working assay as harmful, and in particular do not distinguish an activator, which raises activity, from an inhibitor, which lowers it.

concept_tested: Interpreting the plateau of an enzyme saturation curve
stem: In the enzyme-velocity graph shown, the curve becomes nearly horizontal at high substrate concentration. What does this plateau indicate?

options.A: Nearly all active sites of the available enzyme molecules are occupied
options.B: The substrate has converted the enzyme into a lipid
options.C: The reaction has become independent of enzyme concentration at every substrate level
options.D: The enzyme has necessarily been denatured by high temperature

correct_answer_text: Nearly all active sites of the available enzyme molecules are occupied

distractor_rationale.B: The substrate has converted the enzyme into a lipid is a plausible distractor, but it conflicts with the required interpreting the plateau of an enzyme saturation curve and therefore cannot be the single correct response.
distractor_rationale.C: The reaction has become independent of enzyme concentration at every substrate level is a plausible distractor, but it conflicts with the required interpreting the plateau of an enzyme saturation curve and therefore cannot be the single correct response.
distractor_rationale.D: The enzyme has necessarily been denatured by high temperature is a plausible distractor, but it conflicts with the required interpreting the plateau of an enzyme saturation curve and therefore cannot be the single correct response.

solution: At high substrate concentration the fixed amount of enzyme becomes saturated, so nearly all active sites are occupied and adding more substrate produces little further rise in velocity.
formula_principle: A fixed enzyme concentration approaches a maximum velocity when its active sites are saturated.
common_misconception: A plateau from substrate saturation is confused with temperature denaturation.
difficulty_basis: One-step recognition or direct use of a single prescribed fact; low reasoning and distractor load

concept_tested: Inferring persistent activity loss after heating above the optimum
stem: An enzyme follows the temperature-activity curve shown. A sample is heated to 65 degree C and then cooled back to 37 degree C. Why may its original activity fail to return?

options.A: Cooling removes every substrate molecule from the solution
options.B: High temperature may irreversibly alter the enzyme's three-dimensional active site
options.C: The enzyme changes permanently into a carbohydrate at 65 degree C
options.D: Cooling forces all enzyme molecules to bind inhibitors

correct_answer_text: High temperature may irreversibly alter the enzyme's three-dimensional active site

distractor_rationale.A: Cooling removes every substrate molecule from the solution is a plausible distractor, but it conflicts with the required inferring persistent activity loss after heating above the optimum and therefore cannot be the single correct response.
distractor_rationale.C: The enzyme changes permanently into a carbohydrate at 65 degree C is a plausible distractor, but it conflicts with the required inferring persistent activity loss after heating above the optimum and therefore cannot be the single correct response.
distractor_rationale.D: Cooling forces all enzyme molecules to bind inhibitors is a plausible distractor, but it conflicts with the required inferring persistent activity loss after heating above the optimum and therefore cannot be the single correct response.

solution: Heating well above the optimum can denature the protein and alter its active site. Cooling does not necessarily restore that three-dimensional structure.
formula_principle: High temperature can denature an enzyme, whereas ordinary cooling mainly slows molecular movement.
common_misconception: Students assume every temperature effect is fully reversible.

concept_tested: Combining GC percentage with hydrogen-bond counting
stem: A double-stranded DNA segment has 100 base pairs, of which 40 per cent are G-C pairs. How many hydrogen bonds hold the two strands together?

distractor_rationale.A: 180 is a plausible distractor, but it conflicts with the required combining gc percentage with hydrogen-bond counting and therefore cannot be the single correct response.
distractor_rationale.B: 200 is a plausible distractor, but it conflicts with the required combining gc percentage with hydrogen-bond counting and therefore cannot be the single correct response.
distractor_rationale.D: 300 is a plausible distractor, but it conflicts with the required combining gc percentage with hydrogen-bond counting and therefore cannot be the single correct response.

solution: There are 40 G-C pairs and 60 A-T pairs. The total is 40 x 3 + 60 x 2 = 120 + 120 = 240 hydrogen bonds.
formula_principle: Each G-C pair has three hydrogen bonds and each A-T pair has two.
common_misconception: The percentage is applied to individual bases instead of base pairs, or one bond value is used for every pair.

concept_tested: Separating effects of concentration, inhibitor and denaturation
stem: Four assays begin with the same enzyme activity. I receives more enzyme while substrate remains abundant. II receives a specific inhibitor. III is heated to 65 degree C. IV receives more substrate when its enzyme is already saturated. In which assays is activity expected to decrease?

distractor_rationale.A: I and IV only is a plausible distractor, but it conflicts with the required separating effects of concentration, inhibitor and denaturation and therefore cannot be the single correct response.
distractor_rationale.B: I, II and III only is a plausible distractor, but it conflicts with the required separating effects of concentration, inhibitor and denaturation and therefore cannot be the single correct response.
distractor_rationale.C: II and IV only is a plausible distractor, but it conflicts with the required separating effects of concentration, inhibitor and denaturation and therefore cannot be the single correct response.

solution: A specific inhibitor lowers activity and heating to 65 degree C can denature the enzyme. More enzyme with abundant substrate increases capacity, while more substrate at saturation causes little change rather than a decrease.
formula_principle: Enzyme activity is reduced by inhibitors and denaturing temperatures; saturation limits the effect of additional substrate.
common_misconception: A plateau is treated as a fall in activity, or adding enzyme is assumed to dilute the reaction.
